validated_results.title: Consumption of Ultra-Processed Foods and Increased Risks of Prostate Cancer in a Random Sample of United States Adults.
validated_results.reason: Original human study of dietary ultra-processed food intake and prostate cancer risk in a nationally representative United States sample, providing a target-specific quantitative estimate.

extraction.comparison_type: Combined second, third and fourth quartiles of ultra-processed food intake (% of total energy) versus lowest quartile
extraction.population: Male adults in the United States National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 2003-2023

sample_size.excerpt: Among 17,024 male adults, compared to those in the lowest, participants in the combined second, third, and fourth quartiles had a significant 29% higher risk of prostate cancer (p = 0.031), while those in the combined third and fourth quartiles had a significant 30% higher risk (p=0.035). Perhaps due to smaller sample sizes, those in the fourth quartile had a possible but non-significant increase of 31% (p=0.079).

effect_size.excerpt: In adjusted analyses, corresponding values were 27% (p=0.045), 31% (p=0.037), and 34% (p=0.072). In these data, people with higher ultra-processed food intake had higher risks of prostate cancer.

confidence_interval.excerpt: We used 90% confidence intervals to test for significance as harm was prespecified.

p_value.excerpt: In adjusted analyses, corresponding values were 27% (p=0.045), 31% (p=0.037), and 34% (p=0.072).

comparison.excerpt: compared to those in the lowest, participants in the combined second, third, and fourth quartiles had a significant 29% higher risk of prostate cancer

design.excerpt: We used nationally representative data from the United States National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey from 2003 to 2023.

continent.excerpt: a Random Sample of United States Adults

location.excerpt: United States National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey

exposure_measurement.excerpt: Ultra processed food intake was estimated from two 24-hour dietary recalls using the validated and widely used NOVA classification and categorized into quartiles based on the percentage of total energy intake.
